page_placements.theme: Frequency, variance and learning conditions influence feature allocation

record.tranche_reason: The post reports measurements and evaluations of SAE features and residual activations in language models, bearing on indirect evidence for SAE-recoverable features in LLMs. It does not test toy-model superposition.
record.gate_note: Rows below cover reported evaluations of SAE feature quality and feature properties relevant to V4. The residual-to-unigram cosine results, reconstruction losses, and training-speed results are not rows: they do not measure whether SAE features are recoverable representation units. The post does not test feature competition, overlap geometry, or dimensionality.
record.test_reason: This is a methods post proposing tokenized SAEs (a per-token decoder lookup table). It uses SAEs as a tool and reports mainly its own architecture's performance against baselines: CE loss, NMSE, training speed and feature-complexity scores. None of its results bear on whether features are superposed in toy models (V1), on capacity-driven or other origins of polysemanticity (V2, V3), on whether LLMs contain SAE-recoverable sparse features (V4), on SAE features being canonical units (V5), or on feature dimensionality (V6). The side findings, that public SAE features are often unigram-reconstruction features and that residuals resemble unigram residuals, concern a related but different construct. They are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that adding a per-token decoder lookup table gives a Pareto improvement in CE/NMSE over TopK and ReLU SAEs, with about 8x faster training. It also yields fewer unigram-based 'simple' features and similarly interpretable features. They argue token subspaces stay salient even in Gemma 2B. They note a limited feature-quality sample, more dead features, and the need for further investigation.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains tokenized sparse autoencoders with per-token decoder lookup biases; it does not use the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that SAE feature patterns vary with layer and architecture; it also notes that its feature-complexity measures may be inexact.

fits_no_version.finding: In public RES-JB layer 8, 76% of features are activated by a unigram. Authors attribute the many unigram-reconstruction features to an n-gram frequency imbalance in SAE training. Reconstruction MSE falls with token frequency.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE dictionaries are shaped by training-data token frequency, so many learned features are unigram-reconstruction artifacts rather than model-intrinsic units.

fits_no_version.finding: Residual activations have high cosine similarity to the residuals of their last-token unigram across GPT-2, Pythia and Gemma 2B, even in late layers. Trigrams approximate GPT-2 small residuals well.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A large share of LLM residual-stream variance lies in a token-identity subspace.

record.problems: The manual feature-quality sample is limited to 20 features; the authors explicitly urge caution. The feature-complexity measures are described as inexact, and plotted comparisons lack numerical values in the text. The study does not test whether SAE features are complete, stable, or canonical units of the underlying model.
record.rows_left_out: No more than 60 rows were reported. Reconstruction, CE loss, training speed, and residual-to-unigram cosine results were left out because they do not directly measure the V4 outcome of SAE feature recoverability.

untested.parts: No toy models; no sparsity transition or geometry.
No analysis of non-capacity origins of polysemanticity.
Does not test whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or whether sparse features are genuinely recoverable. SAEs are assumed as a tool.
No test of completeness, stability or canonicity. There is only an indirect argument that SAE features reflect training-frequency imbalance.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' is incorrect: the post is an SAE-architecture contribution, and nearly all rows compare the authors' method with baselines. The feature-quality rubric covers only 20 features. A comment notes a bug in the expansion-sweep runs, where the lookup table was not learned.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity or gives important features dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises without capacity pressure.
Does not establish that SAE features are ground-truth features of the model, or test how broadly features are distributed across neurons.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

relation.reason: Uses SAE dictionary representations to develop and evaluate a reconstruction method without testing the listed claims about superposition or canonical representational units.

tranche.reason: The post develops a tokenized SAE method and evaluates reconstruction, training speed and feature quality. Its unigram-response measurements concern SAE feature character and do not directly test a listed superposition claim version.

source_check.notes: The 39% and 66% figures use the unigram-activated subset as their denominator. The training-frequency explanation is the authors' attribution; these measurements do not establish it causally.
